lessons.title: What makes a prompt work
lessons.eli5: Think of Claude as a smart temp worker on their first day: quick and capable, but brand new to your world. A good prompt is the briefing you'd give them — the task, the background, who it's for, and what the finished result should look like.
lessons.body:
## The brilliant new colleague

Anthropic's own prompting guide suggests a useful mental model: treat Claude as a **brilliant but brand-new colleague** who has no background on your team, your norms or your goals. Claude is very capable, but it can only work with what you put in front of it. When an output disappoints, the cause is usually not that Claude "can't do it". The cause is that the request left out something a new colleague would have needed.

Anthropic calls the quick test for this the "golden rule": show your prompt to a colleague who has minimal context on the task. If they would be confused or would have to guess, Claude will be confused or will guess too.

## The six building blocks

Most strong business prompts contain some version of these parts. Not every prompt needs all six, but when an output misses, check this list first.

| Building block | The question it answers | Example (writing a project update) |
|---|---|---|
| **Task** | What exactly should Claude produce? | "Write a status update email for the website relaunch." |
| **Context** | What background does Claude need, and why does this matter? | "The launch slipped two weeks because the payment vendor was late. Leadership is nervous after last quarter's outage." |
| **Audience** | Who will read or use the output? | "The executive team. They read on their phones between meetings." |
| **Constraints** | What limits or rules apply? | "About 150 words. Don't name the vendor. Don't promise a new date we haven't confirmed." |
| **Output format** | What shape should the answer take? | "Subject line, three short bullets (status, risk, ask), then one closing sentence." |
| **Examples** | What does good look like? | "Here is last month's update, which the CEO liked. Match its tone." |

You can also give Claude a **role or perspective** ("You are an experienced HR business partner reviewing this policy for clarity") when a particular expertise or tone would help. A role sharpens focus, but it is not a replacement for context. A role with no facts behind it still produces generic output.

## Explicit beats implied

Claude follows what you ask for. If you want more than the obvious minimum, say so. Compare these two requests:

```text
Weak:   Make this better.

Strong: Shorten this announcement to about 150 words for busy
        executives. Open with the decision we need from them
        (approve the Q3 budget by Friday), then give the two
        reasons. Keep a confident but not salesy tone.
```

"Better" could mean shorter, friendlier, more formal, more persuasive or more detailed. Claude will pick one interpretation, and it may not be yours. The strong version names the length, the audience, what goes first and the tone. Nothing is left to guess. One nuance: models don't count words exactly, so when length truly matters, ask for a set number of sentences, bullets or paragraphs — those limits hold better than word counts.

Two more habits:

- **Explain the why.** "Keep it under 150 words *because people read it on their phones*" works better than a bare rule. When Claude knows the reason, it can apply the spirit of it to cases you didn't foresee.
- **Say what to do, not only what to avoid.** "Write in flowing paragraphs" steers better than "don't use bullet points".

## Supply your facts; don't expect Claude to know them

Claude has broad general knowledge, but it does **not** know your internal facts unless you provide them: your pricing, your policies, last week's meeting, your product roadmap. If you ask "summarize our refund policy" without attaching the policy, Claude may produce something plausible and generic, which is worse than useless because it *looks* right.

Give Claude the source material instead: paste the text, upload the document, or work inside a Project that already holds the files. Then tell it to work from that material.

## Make it safe for Claude to say "I don't know"

Language models can produce confident, specific-sounding details that are wrong (more on this in Domain 2). You can lower the risk in the prompt itself:

- "Answer **only** from the attached policy. If the policy doesn't cover a question, say so instead of guessing."
- "If you are unsure about a figure, flag it with [CHECK] rather than estimating."
- For very long documents (20,000+ tokens, roughly 30+ pages): "First quote the passages that are relevant, then answer based on those quotes."

These instructions reduce invented details. They do **not** remove the need to check important facts yourself.

## Worked example: an HR request

**First attempt:** "Write a job ad for a project coordinator."

The result is fine but generic. It could be for any company, it lists made-up perks and it's twice as long as the team's normal ads.

**Improved prompt:**

```text
Write a job ad for a Project Coordinator on our events team.

Context: We're a 60-person nonprofit that runs community health
fairs. The role is hybrid (2 days a week in our Leeds office).
The salary band and benefits are in the attached sheet. Use only
those benefits; don't add any others.

Audience: early-career candidates, many of them from outside the
nonprofit sector.

Format: a headline, a 2-sentence intro, "What you'll do" (5
bullets), "What you'll bring" (4 bullets), then how to apply.
About 300 words.

Tone: warm and plain-spoken. Our last ad is pasted below as a
tone reference. Don't copy its content.
```

Every gap from the first attempt now has a matching instruction. That is the habit the exam rewards: **diagnose which ingredient is missing, then add exactly that ingredient**.
keyTakeaways: Treat Claude like a brilliant new colleague with no background: it can only use what you give it.
A strong prompt covers the task, context (including why), audience, constraints, output format and, when useful, examples.
Be explicit: name the length, audience, structure and tone instead of saying "make it better".
Explain the reason behind a rule, and say what to do rather than only what to avoid.
Supply internal facts (policies, data, notes) yourself. Claude does not know them otherwise.
Allow Claude to say it doesn't know, or to work only from the provided material, to reduce invented details.
examTips: When a question shows a weak prompt and asks for the best fix, pick the option that adds the missing ingredient (context, audience, format, source material), not the one that rewords politely or adds urgency.
If the output is generic, the likely missing piece is context or source material. If the length or shape is wrong, the missing piece is the output format or constraints.
Options that say "tell Claude to be more accurate" or "tell Claude to try harder" are weaker than options that give Claude specific information or criteria.
Expect business scenarios (HR, marketing, operations, education) rather than technical ones. The principle is the same either way.
commonTraps: Assuming a role alone ("You are a marketing expert") fixes a generic output. Without facts and audience, the role adds little.
Expecting Claude to know company-internal facts, such as current prices or policies, without providing them.
Switching to a different model or tool when the real problem is a vague prompt.
Writing only negative rules ("don't be wordy, don't use jargon") instead of describing the target ("plain English, 3 short paragraphs").
Treating an "answer only from the document" instruction as a guarantee of accuracy. It reduces risk; it doesn't replace checking.

lessons.title: Structuring longer prompts
lessons.eli5: It's like handing a new colleague a tall stack of papers with your request scribbled on some page in the middle — they can't tell your instructions apart from the paperwork. Add labelled dividers ("background here, documents there, examples there") and put your request on the last page, so it's obvious what's the job and what's just material to read.
lessons.body:
## Why structure matters once prompts get long

A two-line request rarely needs structure. Problems start when a prompt mixes several kinds of content: your instructions, background, a long document, some examples and the question itself. Claude then has to work out which sentences are *orders* and which are *material*. If a pasted email says "please reply by Friday", is that an instruction to Claude, or text to be summarized?

Clear structure removes that ambiguity.

## Technique 1: Separate instructions from material

Label each part so nothing blends together. You can use plain headings, or simple tags in angle brackets, which Anthropic's guidance recommends for complex prompts:

```text
<instructions>
Summarize the customer feedback below for the product team.
Group comments by theme and count how many mention each theme.
</instructions>

<feedback>
[paste 120 survey comments here]
</feedback>
```

The tag names are not magic words. Claude doesn't need a special list of approved tags. What matters is that they are **descriptive and used consistently**, so the boundary between "what to do" and "what to work on" is obvious. Headings such as "INSTRUCTIONS" and "SURVEY COMMENTS" do the same job.

When you include several documents, label each one and say where it came from ("Document 1: 2025 staff handbook", "Document 2: draft 2026 handbook"). Then you can refer to them precisely: "List every change between Document 1 and Document 2."

## Technique 2: Long material first, question last

For long inputs (a report, a contract, a long transcript), Anthropic recommends putting the **long material near the top** and the **question or instructions at the end**. Its documentation reports that putting the query after the documents improved response quality by up to 30% in its tests, especially with complex inputs made up of several documents.

| Layout | Effect |
|---|---|
| Question, then 40 pages of documents | The question is far away from where Claude finishes reading. |
| 40 pages of documents, then question | Claude reads the material, then meets the task with everything fresh. |

A helpful addition for long documents (Anthropic's docs mention this especially for documents over roughly 20,000 tokens) is to ask Claude to **pull out the relevant quotes first**, then answer based on them. This keeps the answer tied to the actual text.

## Technique 3: Show examples (few-shot prompting)

When **format, tone or style** matters, an example often beats a paragraph of description. Showing a few samples of good output is called *few-shot* or *multishot* prompting.

Anthropic's guidance says good examples are:

- **Relevant**: they look like your real task.
- **Varied**: they differ from each other, so Claude learns the pattern instead of copying one sample. If all three sample product descriptions open with "Introducing…", expect every new one to open that way too.
- **Clearly marked**: label them as examples so Claude doesn't confuse them with instructions or with material to process.

The docs suggest roughly **3–5 examples** for best results. In everyday business prompting even one or two good samples help a lot. You can also ask Claude to review your examples for variety, or to draft more in the same style.

```text
Write a two-sentence description for each new course in the
list below. Match the style of these examples:

<examples>
<example>
Excel for Busy Managers: Build the three reports your team
actually asks for, in under an hour a week. No formulas
memorized, no macros, just practical shortcuts.
</example>
<example>
Difficult Conversations: Practise the openings that keep
feedback calm and specific. Leave with a script you can use
on Monday.
</example>
</examples>

<courses>
[list of new course titles]
</courses>
```

## Technique 4: Number the steps when order matters

If Claude must do things in sequence, write the steps as a numbered list: "1. Remove duplicates. 2. Group by region. 3. Flag any region with fewer than five responses." Anthropic's guidance recommends numbered steps when the order of the steps matters.

## Putting it together

A well-structured long prompt usually reads in this order:

1. A one-line role or purpose (optional).
2. Background and context.
3. The long material, labelled.
4. Examples of good output, labelled.
5. The specific task, steps and output format, last.

## Worked example: an operations summary

**Before:** a manager pastes three supplier contracts and writes "compare these" at the top. The answer mixes up which clause belongs to which supplier and ignores the question that matters to them, which is termination terms.

**After:**

- Each contract is labelled with the supplier name.
- The instructions come after the contracts: "For each supplier, quote the termination clause, then give the notice period and any exit fee in a table with one row per supplier. If a contract has no exit fee, write 'none stated'."

The fix wasn't a smarter model. The fix was making it obvious which text was which and what the deliverable looked like.
keyTakeaways: Separate instructions from material with clear labels, headings or descriptive tags, and use them consistently.
With long documents, put the material first and the question or instructions at the end.
Asking Claude to extract relevant quotes first keeps answers about long documents grounded in the text.
Use examples (few-shot) when format or tone matters. Make them relevant, varied and clearly labelled. The docs suggest about 3–5.
Use numbered steps when the order of the steps matters.
examTips: If a scenario says Claude confused pasted content with instructions, or mixed up multiple documents, the answer is clearer separation and labelling.
If outputs vary in format from run to run, adding examples of the target format is usually the best fix.
If outputs all copy one sample too closely, the fix is more varied examples, not removing examples entirely.
Remember the order for long inputs: documents first, question last.
commonTraps: Believing only certain "official" tag names work. Any clear, consistent label does the job.
Giving one example and then being surprised that every output imitates it word for word.
Burying the actual question at the top of a very long prompt, above pages of pasted material.
Writing a long paragraph describing a format when a short example would show it instantly.

lessons.title: Breaking big requests into steps
lessons.eli5: You wouldn't hand a builder one instruction — "build me a house" — and walk away. You'd agree the plan first, then check the foundations before the walls go up. Big Claude tasks work the same way: small steps, with a check after each one.
lessons.body:
## The one-giant-prompt problem

Suppose a marketing lead types: *"Research our three main competitors, analyze their pricing, write a positioning strategy and draft a launch email."* Claude will produce something, but:

- The competitor facts may be thin or wrong, and the strategy is built on top of them.
- If the email misses the mark, it's hard to tell whether the problem was the research, the analysis or the drafting.
- The answer is long, so mistakes hide in the middle of it.

**Task decomposition** means splitting a complex job into smaller steps, running each one, and checking the result before it feeds the next. Anthropic's prompting guide describes the general pattern as **prompt chaining**: the output of one step becomes the input of the next, with a check in between where useful. The trade is a little more time for a lot more accuracy and control.

## A typical sequence

| Step | What you ask | What you check before moving on |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Gather | "Collect the key facts about X from these sources." | Are the facts right? Is anything missing? |
| 2. Outline | "Propose an outline or plan. Don't write it yet." | Is the structure right? Is the emphasis right? |
| 3. Draft | "Write section 1 based on the approved outline." | Tone, accuracy, length. |
| 4. Review | "Review the draft against these criteria and list problems." | Do you agree with the critique? |
| 5. Finalize | "Apply fixes 1, 3 and 4; ignore 2." | Final read before sending. |

Each step is small enough to check quickly. A wrong fact found in step 1 costs one minute to fix. The same fact found inside a finished strategy document costs an hour.

## Technique: plan first, then execute

One of the simplest and most useful forms of decomposition is to ask Claude to **plan before doing**:

```text
I need a training workshop on giving feedback, for new team
leads (half a day, 12 people).

Before writing anything, propose an agenda: sessions, timings,
and the goal of each session. Wait for my approval before
writing materials.
```

You review the agenda, adjust it ("swap sessions 2 and 3; cut the icebreaker to 10 minutes"), then ask Claude to write the materials **one session at a time**. You stay in control of the direction, and Claude spends its effort on an agreed plan.

## Ways to split a task

- **By stage**: research, then analysis, then writing, then review (the sequence above).
- **By section**: one prompt per chapter or section of a long report, working from the same agreed outline.
- **By item**: process each of 20 customer interviews on its own, then combine the summaries in a final step.
- **By role**: draft in one step, then ask Claude to critique the draft from a specific reader's point of view in another.

## Why decomposition improves quality

1. **Errors become visible.** Each output is short enough to actually read and check.
2. **Each step gets full attention.** A focused prompt with one job usually does that job better than a long prompt juggling five.
3. **You can fix one step without redoing everything.** If the outline is wrong, you fix the outline and regenerate the draft. The research stays as it was.
4. **Human judgment lands where it matters.** Your approval at checkpoints (the plan, key facts) is cheap and high-value.

## When *not* to decompose

Decomposition has a cost: more turns, more of your time. A short email, a quick rewrite or a simple question doesn't need five steps. Use it when the task:

- has several distinct stages (find, analyze, write),
- produces something long or high-stakes,
- needs a human decision partway through, or
- has failed as a single prompt.

## Worked example: a quarterly business review deck

**Single prompt (fails):** "Using the attached sales data, write our QBR presentation." The result has a misread trend and slides in an odd order, and it's hard to know which numbers to trust.

**Decomposed:**

1. "From the attached sales data, list the five most important trends, each with the figures that support it." *You find one misread figure and correct it.*
2. "Propose a 10-slide outline for the leadership audience, built on these corrected trends." *You reorder two slides.*
3. "Write the content for slides 1–5 following the outline." Then slides 6–10.
4. "Act as a skeptical CFO. List the three hardest questions this deck would get." *You add a backup slide.*

Same Claude, same data. The difference is checkpoints and focused steps.

## Connecting to the bigger picture

At larger scale, long multi-step automations with tools and many stages are built by developers and architects. For an Associate, decomposition happens **inside your own conversations and Projects**: plan, run each step, check, then move on.
keyTakeaways: Decomposition splits a complex job into smaller steps and checks each output before it feeds the next one (prompt chaining).
Ask Claude for a plan or outline first, approve or adjust it, then execute it section by section.
Smaller steps make errors visible, give each step full focus and let you fix one stage without redoing everything.
Common splits: by stage, by section, by item, or by role (draft, then critique).
Don't over-decompose simple tasks. Use it for multi-stage, long, high-stakes or previously failing work.
examTips: When a scenario describes one huge prompt producing a muddled or error-prone result, the answer is usually to break it into steps with review points.
"Ask for an outline or plan first, then build on it" is a classic correct answer for long documents.
Look for answers that put a human check at the step where errors would spread downstream, such as facts and research.
An option that adds more instructions to the same giant prompt is usually weaker than splitting the task.
commonTraps: Thinking a longer, more detailed single prompt solves a multi-stage task as well as splitting it does.
Decomposing but never checking the intermediate outputs, which lets errors flow straight through.
Splitting trivial tasks into many steps, which adds time without improving quality.
Assuming decomposition needs technical tools or automation. In a normal Claude conversation it is simply a sequence of focused turns.

lessons.title: Iterating to improve output
lessons.eli5: If a haircut comes out wrong, you don't walk out and come back hoping for a different result. You say "shorter at the sides, keep the top". Improving Claude's output works the same way: spot exactly what's off and say so.
lessons.body:
## First drafts are a starting point

Even a well-written prompt won't always give you exactly what you want on the first try. That's normal. The skill being tested is **what you do next**. There are two broad options:

- **Regenerate blindly**: resend the same prompt unchanged and hope.
- **Iterate deliberately**: work out *what* is wrong, then change the prompt or give feedback that targets that specific problem.

Regenerating occasionally gives a better draft by chance, but it doesn't fix the cause. If the prompt lacked context, every regeneration lacks the same context.

## Step 1: Diagnose what's wrong

Before changing anything, name the failure. Most disappointing outputs fall into one of a few buckets, and each bucket points to a different fix:

| What you see | Likely cause | Targeted fix |
|---|---|---|
| Generic, could be about any company | Missing context or source material | Add background, attach the document, explain the situation |
| Wrong length or shape | Format not specified | State the structure and sections. For length, sentence or paragraph limits work better than word counts — Claude counts tokens, not words |
| Wrong tone | Audience not stated | Name the reader and what they care about. Add a tone sample |
| Invented or wrong facts | No source material, or no permission to say "unknown" | Provide the source. Tell Claude to answer only from it and flag gaps |
| Misses part of the request | Too many things asked at once | Decompose, or number the requirements |
| Inconsistent from run to run | Format described but not shown | Add a few varied examples (docs suggest 3–5) |
| Copies your example too closely | Only one example, or examples too alike | Add varied examples. Say which features to keep |

## Step 2: Give specific feedback

Within a conversation, Claude can revise based on feedback. Specific feedback works; vague feedback doesn't.

```text
Vague:    That's not quite right, try again.

Specific: Keep sections 1 and 2 as they are. Rewrite section 3
          for a non-technical reader: no acronyms, and explain
          "churn" the first time it appears. Cut the conclusion
          to two sentences.
```

Good feedback says **what to keep**, **what to change** and **what "better" means**. It's the same discipline as giving feedback to a colleague.

## Step 3: Change one thing at a time when testing

When you're refining a prompt you'll reuse (a weekly report template, say), change one ingredient per attempt where you can. If you add an audience, a format and three examples all at once and the output improves, you won't know which change mattered, or whether one of them made something else worse.

## Step 4: Judge against clear criteria

"Is this better?" is easier to answer when you have defined what good looks like *before* you start. For a recurring task, write down 3–5 checks:

- Under 200 words?
- Opens with the decision needed?
- Every figure matches the source spreadsheet?
- Readable by someone outside the team?

Run your prompt on a few real inputs and check each output against the list. Anthropic's documentation recommends defining success criteria that are **specific and measurable** in the same way. Business users can apply this informally with a simple checklist.

## Step 5: Know when to start fresh

If a conversation has gone around in circles, with many corrections, contradictory instructions and drafts piling up, it's often better to **start a new conversation** with an improved prompt that includes everything you learned. Long, tangled threads can carry earlier wrong turns forward, and recall degrades as a conversation grows. Take the lessons, not the clutter.

## Step 6: Save what works

When a prompt reliably produces good output, don't lose it:

- Save it as a **template** with blanks for the parts that change.
- Put durable guidance (house style, audience, standard format) into **Project instructions**, so every conversation in that Project starts with it.
- Share it with your team so everyone benefits from the iteration you've already done.

## Worked example: a monthly newsletter

| Round | What happened | Change made |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | "Write our monthly staff newsletter." Bland, invented events. | Attached the list of real events and announcements. Told Claude to use only those. |
| 2 | Accurate but long and formal. | Set a paragraph cap rather than a word count, friendly tone, named the audience (frontline retail staff reading on their phones). |
| 3 | Better, but every item is the same length. | Specified: lead story ~150 words, three short items, one "shout-out". |
| 4 | Good. | Saved as a template in the Internal Comms Project instructions. |

Four rounds, each targeting one diagnosed problem. Retrying the round-1 prompt would never have got there, because the real events weren't in it.

## Iteration has limits

If you've clearly provided the context, format and examples and the output is still wrong, the problem may not be the prompt. The task may need a different feature (research mode for current, multi-source information), a different model, or human expertise. Those cases are covered in the troubleshooting domain.
keyTakeaways: Diagnose the specific failure (context, format, tone, facts, scope, consistency) before changing anything.
Targeted changes beat blind regeneration. A retry doesn't add missing context.
Good feedback says what to keep, what to change and what "better" means.
When refining a reusable prompt, change one thing at a time and judge against criteria written down in advance.
Restart with a clean, improved prompt when a thread gets tangled. Carry the lessons over, not the clutter.
Save prompts that work as templates or Project instructions so the whole team benefits.
examTips: If a question offers "regenerate the response" next to "add the missing audience and format details", the targeted change is almost always correct.
Match the symptom to the fix: generic output means add context, inconsistent format means add examples, invented facts means supply a source and allow "I don't know".
Answers that save a proven prompt as a reusable template or Project instruction are strong for recurring tasks.
When the prompt is already complete and output is still poor, look for answers that change the feature, model or escalation path rather than rewording again.
commonTraps: Clicking retry repeatedly on a prompt that's missing key information.
Giving vague feedback such as "make it better" or "not quite".
Changing many things at once, then not knowing which change helped.
Continuing to patch a very long, contradictory conversation instead of starting fresh with a clean prompt.
Re-solving the same prompt problem every week instead of saving the working version.

lessons.title: Prompting by task type
lessons.eli5: You ask a helpful friend for quick ideas differently than you'd ask them to look something up, explain some numbers, or write a note for you — same friend, different ask. Claude is like that: brainstorming, research, analysis and drafting each work best when you shape the request to the job.
lessons.body:
## One tool, four very different jobs

The exam names four task types: **analysis, research, drafting and brainstorming**. The basic ingredients of a good prompt (task, context, audience, format) apply to all of them, but each type has its own emphasis and its own failure mode.

| Task type | Goal | Key prompt ingredients | Typical failure if you don't adapt |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Analysis** | Make sense of information you already have | The data, the criteria or question, a request for reasoning plus a clear conclusion | A vague summary with no verdict, or a conclusion with no visible reasoning |
| **Research** | Find and gather information you don't have | Scope, sources and time frame, a request for citations, research mode, then verification | Confident claims with no sources, or out-of-date information |
| **Drafting** | Produce a finished piece of writing | Audience, purpose, tone, length, structure, a sample | Generic text in the wrong voice or length |
| **Brainstorming** | Generate many possibilities | Quantity, variety, deferred judgment, then a separate step to evaluate | A few safe, similar ideas, judged too early |

## Analysis

Analysis works on material you provide: a spreadsheet, survey results, a contract, meeting notes.

- **Give the data and the question.** "Which of our five regions is underperforming on repeat purchases, and what's the likely reason?" beats "analyze this".
- **State the criteria.** If you're comparing vendors, say what matters: price, contract length, support hours, data location.
- **Ask for reasoning, then a conclusion.** For multi-step problems, asking Claude to think it through step by step before concluding tends to improve the result, and it lets you check the logic.
- **Ask it to separate facts from interpretation.** "Mark which points come directly from the data and which are your inferences."

```text
Here are the results of our employee engagement survey (attached).
Compare the scores for the four departments on the five questions
about workload. Work through the comparison step by step, then give
a short conclusion: which department most needs attention, and why.
Mark anything that is your interpretation rather than a number from
the data.
```

## Research

Research means gathering information from outside your own materials.

- **Use the right feature.** For questions that need current or multi-source information, Claude's **research mode** is the built-in feature for the job: it searches sources and returns an answer with citations you can check. A plain chat without web access relies on what Claude learned in training, which has a cutoff date.
- **Define the scope.** Time frame, geography, types of sources, what's out of scope.
- **Ask for sources and for gaps.** "Cite a source for each claim, and tell me where you couldn't find good evidence."
- **Verify.** Citations make checking easy, but they don't make checking optional. Open the key sources, especially for figures and anything going to an external or high-stakes audience. (Domain 2 covers this in depth.)
- **Point it at internal knowledge when relevant.** If connectors or Project files hold internal documents, say so: "Use the documents in this Project as well as public sources."

## Drafting

Drafting produces something people will read: emails, reports, announcements, lesson plans, proposals.

- **Audience and purpose first.** Who reads it, and what should they do or feel afterwards?
- **Tone and length.** "Warm, plain English, no more than three short paragraphs." (Sentence or paragraph limits steer length more reliably than word counts.)
- **Structure.** Headline, sections, bullet limits, call to action.
- **A sample.** A previous piece that worked is the fastest way to convey voice.
- **Source facts.** Attach the real details (dates, names, figures) so Claude doesn't fill gaps with invented specifics.
- **Iterate section by section** for long documents (see decomposition).

## Brainstorming

Brainstorming is the one task where **quantity and variety** matter more than polish.

- **Ask for many options.** "Give me 20 ideas", not "give me an idea".
- **Ask for range.** "Include some safe options, some unusual ones, and a few that would need more budget."
- **Defer judgment.** Don't ask for the "best" idea in the same breath. Generating and evaluating at once tends to give safe, similar ideas.
- **Then converge in a separate step.** "Group these into themes" or "Score the top eight against cost, effort and audience fit."
- **Give constraints that genuinely apply** (budget, brand rules, timing). Leave out ones that don't, so they don't box the ideas in.

```text
Brainstorm 20 ideas for increasing attendance at our monthly
all-hands meeting (300 staff, mostly remote). Range from small
tweaks to bold changes. Don't evaluate them yet.

[next turn]
Now group the ideas into 4-5 themes, and pick the 3 with the best
impact for the least effort. Explain each choice in one line.
```

## Mixed tasks

Real work often combines types: research a market, *analyze* what you find, *brainstorm* positioning options, then *draft* a pitch. Treat each type as its own step with its own prompt. This is decomposition (task 1.2) and task-type adaptation (task 1.4) working together.

## Quick decision guide

- "I have the information; I need to understand it." → **Analysis**: data plus criteria, reasoning plus a conclusion.
- "I don't have the information yet." → **Research**: research mode, scope, citations, verification.
- "I know what to say; I need it written well." → **Drafting**: audience, tone, length, sample.
- "I need options." → **Brainstorming**: many varied ideas, evaluated afterwards.
keyTakeaways: Analysis: provide the data and criteria, and ask for step-by-step reasoning that ends in a clear conclusion. Ask Claude to separate facts from inferences.
Research: use research mode for current or multi-source questions, define the scope, require citations, and verify key claims yourself.
Drafting: lead with audience and purpose, then tone, length, structure, a sample and the real facts.
Brainstorming: ask for many varied options, hold off on judging them, then evaluate or cluster in a separate step.
Mixed jobs combine types. Run each type as its own step.
examTips: Identify the task type in the scenario first, then pick the answer whose prompt strategy fits that type.
For research questions, strong answers involve research mode or web sources with citations plus human verification. Weak answers trust a plain chat's memory for current facts.
For brainstorming, the correct answer usually asks for many varied ideas and evaluates them later, not "give me the single best idea".
For analysis, look for answers that supply the actual data and criteria and ask for reasoning, not "summarize this".
commonTraps: Asking Claude to brainstorm and pick the winner in one step, which narrows ideas too early.
Treating citations as proof. Linked sources still need a check for high-stakes use.
Using a plain chat without web access for questions about recent events or current figures.
Drafting without stating the audience, then blaming the model for the wrong tone.
Asking for analysis without saying what question it should answer or what criteria matter.

lessons.title: Prompting drill: fix the weak prompt
lessons.eli5: Think of a recipe that came out tasting wrong. You fix it by tasting, spotting the missing ingredient, and adding just that — not by buying a new oven or shouting at the cook. Exam questions reward the same move: the small, specific addition (who it's for, what shape, an example) usually beats the big dramatic change.
lessons.body:
## How Domain 1 questions are built

Domain 1 questions usually describe a person in a business role, a request they made, and what went wrong. They then ask for the **best next step** or the **most effective change**. Several options will sound reasonable. The correct one usually:

1. **Targets the actual cause** of the problem described.
2. **Adds the missing ingredient** (context, audience, format, examples, source material, or a step-by-step structure).
3. **Uses the lightest effective fix**: improving the prompt before switching tools, models or platforms.

The wrong options tend to fall into recognisable patterns.

| Distractor pattern | Why it's wrong |
|---|---|
| "Regenerate the response until it's better" | Doesn't fix the cause. The same missing context gives the same kind of output. |
| "Add 'be accurate' / 'try harder' / 'this is important'" | Emphasis without information. Claude still doesn't know what you need. |
| "Switch to a different AI tool" or "use the largest model" | Heavy fix for a prompt problem. A good answer fixes the prompt first. |
| "Give up and do it manually" | Over-correction. The task is suitable; the prompt needs work. |
| "Make the prompt longer" with no specific content | Length isn't the goal. Relevant information is. |

## A three-question elimination funnel

For each option, ask:

1. **Does it address the symptom described?** Wrong tone → audience/tone. Inconsistent format → examples. Invented facts → source material and permission to say "unknown". Muddled multi-part output → decomposition.
2. **Is it specific?** "Specify a 150-word limit and executive audience" beats "clarify expectations".
3. **Is it proportionate?** Prefer a prompt change over a platform change, unless the scenario shows the prompt is already complete.

## Practice scenarios

Work through these yourself before reading the analysis.

### Scenario 1: The off-tone apology

A customer-success manager asks Claude: *"Write an email apologizing for the delayed shipment."* The draft is stiff and formal, and it offers a 20% refund that the company never approved.

**Best fix:** Add the context (premium customer, two-week delay, reason) and the audience and tone (warm, personal), and state the constraint explicitly: *"Offer free express shipping on the next order. Don't offer refunds or other compensation."*
**Why:** Two separate failures (tone and an invented offer) trace to two missing ingredients (audience/tone and constraints). Regenerating would just as likely invent a different offer.

### Scenario 2: The everything report

An operations analyst asks Claude, in one prompt, to review a year of incident logs, find root causes, recommend process changes and write a board summary. The summary contains a root cause that doesn't appear in the logs.

**Best fix:** Decompose. First extract and list the incidents and causes from the logs, then check them. Next analyze the patterns, then recommend changes, and only then draft the board summary from the verified findings.
**Why:** The error came from an unchecked early stage flowing into a polished final output. Checkpoints catch it.

### Scenario 3: The inconsistent product blurbs

A retail marketer generates descriptions for 40 products. Some are one line and some are three paragraphs. Some use bullets and some don't.

**Best fix:** Specify the format (for example, two sentences plus three bullet benefits) and include three to five **varied examples** of finished descriptions.
**Why:** Inconsistent format is the classic signal for examples (few-shot).

### Scenario 4: The safe brainstorm

A teacher asks, *"What's the best way to make my history unit more engaging?"* and gets three conventional suggestions.

**Best fix:** Reframe it as a real brainstorm. Ask for 15–20 varied ideas across different kinds of activity and effort levels, with no evaluation at first. Then, in a follow-up step, ask Claude to rank the ideas against the teacher's class size, time and resources.
**Why:** Asking for "the best" in a single step narrows the options too early.

### Scenario 5: The research that wasn't

A project manager asks in a regular chat for "the latest data protection rules for our industry in Brazil" and gets a confident answer with no sources.

**Best fix:** Use **research mode** (or web search) with a defined scope, ask for citations, and verify the key points with the official source or a qualified colleague before relying on them.
**Why:** It's a research task about current information. It needs sources, and the regulatory stakes need verification. Rewording the chat prompt wouldn't make the information current.

### Scenario 6: The fifth retry

A communications officer has regenerated a speech draft five times. Each version is too long and too technical for a community audience.

**Best fix:** Stop regenerating. Tell Claude exactly what's wrong and what to do: "Six minutes spoken (about 800 words), for local residents with no technical background. Replace jargon with everyday examples. Keep the three main points from version 3."
**Why:** This is iteration with specific feedback. Repeated retries without new information give repeated misses.

## Pattern summary

| Symptom | Missing ingredient | Task |
|---|---|---|
| Generic or invented details | Context and source material | 1.1 |
| Wrong tone or length | Audience, format, constraints | 1.1 |
| Inconsistent format | Examples | 1.1 |
| Errors in multi-stage output | Decomposition with checkpoints | 1.2 |
| Repeated similar misses | Diagnosis plus specific feedback | 1.3 |
| Wrong approach for the job | Task-type strategy (analysis, research, drafting, brainstorm) | 1.4 |

When you're unsure between two good options, pick the one a thoughtful colleague would choose: **give Claude what it was missing, in the smallest change that fixes the cause.**
keyTakeaways: Correct answers target the cause, add the specific missing ingredient and use the lightest effective fix.
Typical distractors: blind regeneration, emphasis words without information, switching tools or models, giving up, or adding length without content.
Map symptom to fix: tone or length → audience and format; inconsistency → examples; invented details → sources; multi-stage errors → decomposition.
Research tasks need research mode or web search, citations and verification. Brainstorms need many varied ideas before judging.
examTips: Read the symptom carefully. The scenario usually shows exactly which ingredient is missing.
Eliminate options that change the platform or model when the prompt is clearly incomplete.
Eliminate options that only add emphasis ("be very careful", "this is urgent").
When two answers both help, prefer the one that is more specific and checkable.
commonTraps: Choosing the most dramatic answer (new tool, biggest model) instead of the most targeted one.
Choosing "do it manually" for a task that is appropriate for Claude and just needs a better prompt.
Missing that a scenario is really a research task needing current, cited information.
Assuming more prompt text automatically means a better prompt.
